  max_capture_body_bytes: 16mb    # per direction per exchange
  max_ws_message_bytes: 16mb      # a WebSocket message, when rules read messages
  max_observer_lag_bytes: 16mb    # how far an observing addon may fall behind
  max_buffered_bytes: 1gb         # all of the above together, across the process

  # connections
  max_connections: 10000
  max_connections_per_client: 10000   # per client IP; defaults to max_connections

  # policy state
  max_metric_keys: 100000
  max_metric_bytes: 256mb
  max_state_entries: 100000
  max_address_list_bytes: 256mb The upstream connection timeout is upstream.connect_timeout
(upstream). Addons have their own limits
(addon limits).
82.title: Limits

83.text:
The timeouts are generous by default. roxy decides what passes, not how
long a well-behaved exchange may take: a model call that takes minutes to
start answering, or a quiet WebSocket, should not hit one. Only
header_timeout is tight, to stop clients that open connections and send
nothing. A long timeout costs a connection slot, not memory, so if idle
connections run out, raise max_connections rather than shortening the
timeouts. If the upstream answers before it has read the whole upload, and then
stops reading it for twice body_idle_timeout, roxy cancels the upload
and records upstream_body_timeout.
83.title: Timeouts

84.text:
max_buffered_bytes bounds everything roxy buffers to inspect or copy:
bodies that rules read, bodies being decoded or signed, WebSocket messages
that rules read, endpoint call bodies, and copies for observing addons.
Each exchange reserves what it needs before it buffers. If the budget
cannot cover a reservation, the exchange fails at once
(buffer_budget_exhausted). Nothing waits and nothing is evicted. A body of unknown length that a rule reads reserves the whole
max_inspect_body_bytes, so the defaults allow 1024 such bodies at once.
The budget is not a cap on the process's memory: socket buffers, streaming
buffers and addon memory are separate.
84.title: Buffer budget

85.text:
A connection over max_connections or max_connections_per_client is
closed at once and logged as connection_refused. The per-client cap
counts TCP peers, so behind a load balancer it counts the load
balancer.The ca_server listener has a separate cap of max_connections.Each HTTP/2 connection can hold up to 4 MiB of request data not yet
sent upstream, outside the buffer budget.Metric and state tables never evict entries
(never evict).
85.title: Connections

86.text:
How clients talk to roxy, how requests are parsed, and what goes to the
upstream and back.
86.title: HTTP

87.text:
modethe client speaksrequest targethttp_proxy (default)HTTP/1.1 to a proxy (HTTP_PROXY / HTTPS_PROXY)absolute-form, or CONNECT and then origin-form inside the tunnelhttpplain HTTP/1.1 to roxy as if it were the serverorigin-form; Host names the target roxy does not authenticate clients. Rules see listener.name and
client.ip. listeners:
  - name: proxy
    mode: http_proxy           # the default
    bind: 0.0.0.0:3128
    quarantine_on:             # optional
      parse_errors: { count: 20, window: 1m }
  - name: gateway
    mode: http
    bind: 0.0.0.0:8080
    forwarded_for:             # optional; mode: http only
      trusted_hops: 1          # the proxies in front of roxy quarantine_on.parse_errors quarantines
roxy once the listener has refused count malformed requests within
window. It needs roxy run --state-dir.
87.title: Listener modes

88.text:
Absolute-form (GET http://host/path HTTP/1.1) is plain HTTP.
Host must match the URL.CONNECT opens a tunnel that roxy inspects (below).Origin-form is refused, except for the host roxy.internal, which
serves the CA at /roxy-ca.pem
(CA distribution).Proxy-Authorization is never forwarded.
88.title: HTTP proxy

89.text:
For a gateway behind a load balancer that terminates TLS
(HTTP gateway). Only origin-form requests are accepted.Host names the target: exactly one, port 80 unless given, scheme
http. Without a redirect the request goes to that host over plain
HTTP.A client that starts a TLS handshake is closed
(tls_on_http_listener).
89.title: HTTP listener

90.text:
Without forwarded_for, client.ip is the TCP peer, which behind a load
balancer is the load balancer. With forwarded_for.trusted_hops: N, each
of the N proxies in front of roxy is taken to append the address it saw
to X-Forwarded-For, so the client is the Nth entry from the right.
Entries further left were written by the client and are ignored. That address is client.ip everywhere: rules, metric keys, addons and
the flow log. The flow log also records the TCP peer as client.peer.A request with fewer entries than hops, or with a trusted entry that is
not a plain IP address, is refused with 400
(forwarded_for_invalid). It is never attributed to the peer instead.The header is forwarded as received. The hop count does not prove that a request came through those proxies.
A client that can reach the listener directly can write its own entries,
so the network must let only the trusted proxies reach the listener.
90.title: Clients behind a load balancer

91.text:
A CONNECT gets 200 Connection Established. Rules decide on the requests
inside the tunnel. The tunnel's first bytes must be: A TLS ClientHello. With tls.require_sni_match (default true) the
SNI must name the CONNECT host (sni_mismatch). roxy terminates TLS
with a certificate for that host, then reads HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2.Plain HTTP, only with http.allow_plain_in_connect (default
false). Anything else is closed, so raw TCP never passes. Requests inside the
tunnel must name the CONNECT host.
91.title: CONNECT

92.text:
roxy offers HTTP/2 inside TLS tunnels (http.enable_h2, default true).
Upstream, it uses HTTP/2 or HTTP/1.1, whichever the origin chooses.
WebSocket upgrades always use HTTP/1.1
(WebSockets).
92.title: HTTP/2

93.text:
roxy does not relay 1xx responses from upstream, such as
103 Early Hints. It sends its own 100 Continue once the rules allow an
upload.
93.title: Informational responses

94.text:
http.allow_response_trailers (default true) forwards an origin's
response trailers, so gRPC works. http.allow_request_trailers (default
false) accepts trailers on requests; without it, a request with trailers
is refused (trailers). Request trailers arrive after the rules have
decided, which is why they are opt-in, and can only be forwarded to an
HTTP/2 origin. A trailer may not carry framing, routing, authentication or content-*
fields. A request with one is refused. A response with one is ended
early, so the client never sees it as complete.
94.title: Trailers

95.text:
A malformed request closes the connection and logs a parse_error event
with a stable reason code. The settings under http: default to strict.
The same checks apply to HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and requests an addon passes on.
95.title: Rejection rules

96.text:
The method is a token of at most 32 bytes.The version is HTTP/1.1. HTTP/1.0 needs http.allow_http10.Lines end in CRLF. A bare LF or CR anywhere in the head is refused.The head is at most limits.max_header_bytes (64 KiB) and the URL at
most limits.max_url_bytes (8 KiB).
96.title: Request line

97.text:
No whitespace before the colon, no folded lines.Values are visible ASCII, space and tab. Control characters are
refused. Bytes above 127 need http.allow_obs_text, and rules read
each as one ISO-8859-1 character.At most limits.max_headers (100) fields.Exactly one Host, matching the URL or the CONNECT host.A host is a DNS name in ASCII (internationalised names as xn--
labels), an IPv4 address, or a bracketed IPv6 address.At most one Content-Length, digits only. A duplicate is refused even
with the same value.Transfer-Encoding, if present, is exactly chunked, and never
together with Content-Length.GET, HEAD, DELETE, OPTIONS and TRACE may carry a body only with
http.allow_body_on_get (body_on_bodiless_method).Expect may only be 100-continue; anything else gets 417.Hop-by-hop fields (Connection and the fields it names, Keep-Alive,
Proxy-Connection, Proxy-Authorization, Proxy-Authenticate, TE,
Trailer, Transfer-Encoding, Upgrade) are never forwarded.
Upgrade is honoured only for a WebSocket a rule allows.
97.title: Headers

98.text: Chunk extensions need http.allow_chunk_extensions.A body is at most limits.max_request_body_bytes (1 GiB).Timeouts are in limits.
98.title: Body

99.text:
The pseudo-headers appear exactly once each, before other headers.Connection-specific headers reset the stream. te is accepted only as
trailers.:path is normalised like an HTTP/1.1 target. :authority must match
the CONNECT host, and so must host if present.limits.h2_max_concurrent_streams and limits.h2_max_header_list_bytes
cap streams per connection and header bytes per stream.
99.title: HTTP/2 requests

100.text:
Applied to the request target, for matching and forwarding alike. The path starts with /. Percent-encodings must be well formed.
[ ] { } | ^ are percent-encoded. Space, control characters, ", <,
>, \, a backtick and non-ASCII are refused.Percent-encoded unreserved characters (A–Z a–z 0–9 - . _ ~) are
decoded. Other encodings stay as they are: %2F stays %2F.Hex digits in the remaining encodings are upper-cased.Dot segments are removed, including encoded ones. A path that climbs
above the root is refused.An empty path becomes /.The query is validated the same way, but nothing in it is decoded.A fragment is refused.The host is lower-cased, its trailing dot removed, and the port made
explicit.
100.title: URL normalisation

101.text:
roxy writes the request out in one canonical form, over HTTP/2 or
HTTP/1.1. Changes made by rules and addons pass the same validation as
the client's request: a header value containing a line break denies the
exchange.
101.title: Upstream requests

102.text:
Upstreams are trusted (threat model), but roxy
re-frames every response: hop-by-hop fields are removed and the framing
rebuilt. Redirects are forwarded, not followed. Compressed bodies pass
through unchanged. Size and time limits are in
limits.
102.title: Responses

103.text:
roxy decodes content-encoding only to inspect a body. body.text and
response.body.text see the decoded text, while the bytes forwarded are
the bytes received (body rules).
Addons are the exception: by default they get decoded bodies
(content codings for addons). roxy decodes gzip, x-gzip, deflate, br and zstd, stacked up to
four deep. Decoding is strict: a truncated or corrupt body cannot be
inspected, and a rule that reads it fails closed. http.strip_accept_encoding (default false) removes accept-encoding
from every request, so origins answer uncompressed.
103.title: Content codings

104.text:
Every refusal roxy makes has the same shape: HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
content-type: application/json
cache-control: no-store
x-roxy-rule: <rule id>
connection: close

{"error":"blocked by roxy","rule":"<rule id>","flow":"<flow id>"} refusalstatusrulea rule denies403, or the rule's deny.statusthe rule idroxy is quarantined403_quarantinedaddress floor403_address_policyunavailable policy input503_fail_closedfailed addon503layer:<name>upstream failure502 (504 for a timeout)none The response never says why. The reason is in the flow log only. A malformed request is refused before any rule sees it, with its reason: HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
content-type: application/json
connection: close

{"error":"rejected by roxy","reason":"cl_and_te"} The status is 400, or a closer one for the reason (413, 414,
431). On HTTP/2 the stream is reset instead. A rule sets the status and message with
deny: { status: 451, message: "..." }. After a deny the connection is
closed, unless the rule says deny: { close: false }. After an upstream
failure the connection stays open.
104.title: Deny responses

105.text:
Metrics count requests or bytes over a sliding window, for rules to
compare against. State is a key/value store that rules write with
set_state and read as state["key"].
105.title: Rate limits and state

106.text:
A metric is defined once and compared in rules, for example
metric.github_writes >= 30. metrics:
  - id: github_writes
    count: requests      # requests | request_bytes | response_bytes | errors | denied | unique(<field>)
    where: host under "api.github.com" and method in [POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE]
    key: [client.ip]     # one count per client; omitted = one count for everything
    window: 1m           # omitted = since start
    max_keys: 10000      # optional; default limits.max_metric_keys count says what is counted. unique(<field>) counts distinct
values, approximately.where says which exchanges count. It can read admission fields,
state and other metrics, but not tags.key gives each distinct value its own count. It takes plain
admission fields such as client.ip or host, not headers.Windows slide in 60 steps, so a 1-minute window moves every second.
A limit can trip up to one step early, never late.Request counts are read before the decision and updated after it, so
metric.x >= 30 denies the 31st request. Denied requests count too.Byte counts grow as bodies stream. A deny that reads one is
checked as bytes arrive, and stops the exchange that crosses the limit.Nullable fields. If a key can be null, such as tls.sni on plain
HTTP, the metric must exclude those exchanges in where
(tls.sni != null), or it does not compile. A rule that reads the
metric needs the same guard.Reload. A metric keeps its counts across a reload if its id,
count, where, key and window are unchanged.
106.title: Metrics

107.text:
Each key value is a separate series, and the number of series is bounded
by limits.max_metric_keys (100 000), each metric's max_keys, and
limits.max_metric_bytes. Nothing is evicted to make room: once a table
is full, any request that needs a new series is denied
(metric_table_full) until old series expire
(never evict). So be careful keying on values the client chooses. host, path, url
and query.raw are all chosen by the client, and denied requests count,
so a client can fill a table keyed on one of them without a single
request being allowed. Limit the values with where: metrics:
  - id: github_requests
    count: requests
    where: host in ["api.github.com", "github.com"]
    key: [host]
    window: 1m host under "github.com" does not limit host, since the client also
chooses subdomains. Where the values cannot be listed, give the metric its
own max_keys, so that filling it only affects that metric. roxy check
warns about a metric keyed on a client-chosen field with no where.
107.title: Key cardinality

108.text:
State is a key/value store shared by all exchanges. Each entry expires
after the rule's ttl, or one hour by default. A rule sees what earlier
exchanges wrote, and, within an exchange, what rules above it wrote. When
the store holds limits.max_state_entries (100 000) entries, a request
that needs a new key is denied (state_unavailable). Addons can read and
write the same store (host services).
108.title: State

109.text:
The protocol between a roxy node (roxy in node mode)
and its control plane. Any server that implements these four operations
can be a control plane. The formal definition is
spec/node-protocol/v1/openapi.yaml,
and each example on this page is titled with the schema it matches. A node enrols once with an enrolment token and gets a node token back. It
then uses the node token to poll for its lease, send its flow log and
renew the token. The lease is the node's whole policy: a roxy.yaml, the
secrets it needs, and how long it is valid. The control plane never
contacts the node; the node always polls.
109.title: Node protocol

110.text:
HTTPS, HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2. All paths start with /roxy/v1/. Bodies are
JSON. Both sides ignore unknown fields.Every request carries Authorization: Bearer <token>: the enrolment
token when enrolling, the node token otherwise. There are no client
certificates, so the control plane can sit behind any TLS terminator.The operator gives the node the control plane's URL, an enrolment
token, and optionally the CA certificates to verify the control plane
with.
110.title: Transport

111.text:
Every error response has a body with a stable error code and a
message. The node acts on the status code, not the body. {"error": "invalid_token", "message": "enrolment token not recognised"} statusmeaningwhat the node does400the request was malformedEnrolment: retries for two minutes, then exits. Renewal: stops renewing. Lease: keeps polling, and the lease expires if this continues.401the token is not recognisedEnrolment: retries for two minutes, then exits. Renewal and flows: retries, since another replica may not know the new token yet. Lease: keeps polling, and the lease expires if this continues. The node never re-enrols by itself.410the node is revokedEnrolment: exits. Otherwise: denies everything at once, forgets its secrets, stops polling, and tries for thirty seconds to send its remaining flow log.426the server will not serve this node's versionEnrolment: exits. Renewal: stops renewing. Lease: treated like 5xx.507the node's flow quota is used upstops sending flows until a new lease arrives5xx, timeout, connection or TLS errorthe control plane is unavailableretries with backoff; the lease expires if this continues
111.title: Errors

112.title: Enrol

113.text:
POST /roxy/v1/renew with the node token and the same body as enrolment.
The response has the same shape as the enrolment response, with the same
node_id and a new token. The server should keep accepting the old
token until its not_after, so that a renewal that reached one replica
but not another does not lock the node out. If the token expires without being renewed, the node exits and needs a
new enrolment token and an empty state dir.
113.title: Renew

114.title: Lease

115.title: Lease body

116.text:
The node sends its protocol_version and roxy_version with every
request. A server that will not serve it answers 426 and lists what the
node lacks: {"error": "unsupported", "message": "roxy 0.1.0 is below this server's floor of 0.2.0", "missing": ["roxy_version:0.2.0"]} There is no other capability negotiation. A lease that uses something the
node does not understand fails to load, and the lease_id on the next
poll shows it was not applied.
116.title: Unsupported versions

117.text:
POST /roxy/v1/flows with the node token. The body may be gzipped, with
Content-Encoding: gzip. {
  "node_id": "node-7f3a9c",
  "lease_id": "lease-01J9Z8K3",
  "seq_first": 1042,
  "events": [
    {"seq": 1042, "ts": "2026-10-06T10:12:00.123Z", "event": "request", "flow": "01J9Z8", "decision": "deny", "terminal_rule": "_default"},
    {"seq": 1043, "ts": "2026-10-06T10:12:00.410Z", "event": "log", "flow": "01J9Z9", "rule": "audit"}
  ]
} fieldmeaningnode_idmust match the token's node, or the answer is 400 node_mismatchlease_idthe lease in force when the batch was put togetherseq_firstthe seq of the first event. Events are numbered consecutively from iteventsflow log records, each with a seq that increases by one per event and keeps increasing across restarts The node sends a batch when it reaches batch_max_bytes, or
flush_interval_seconds after the oldest unsent event. {"acked_through": 1043} Delivery is at least once. The server stores the batch, ignoring events
it already has for that (node_id, seq), and answers with the highest
seq it has stored. The node then discards events up to that number. A
gap in seq within one run means the node dropped events under
on_high_water: spool. Restarts and ship: false also leave gaps. A batch the server refuses with 400 stays queued on the node, so under
hold traffic stops until the server accepts it. A 507 means the
server wants no more flows until it sends a new lease. Other responses
are handled as in the errors table.
117.title: Flow upload

118.text:
The expressions used in a rule's when and a metric's where, and the
actions of a rule's then. How rules are evaluated is in
policy evaluation.
118.title: Rule language

119.text:
Expressions are statically typed, and regular expressions run in linear
time. expr        := or
or          := and ( "or" and )*
and         := not ( "and" not )*
not         := "not" not | primary
primary     := "(" expr ")" | comparison | predicate
comparison  := operand OP operand
predicate   := field | bool                  ; boolean field, or a literal (`where: true`)
operand     := field | field "[" string "]" | literal
OP          := "==" | "!=" | "<" | "<=" | ">" | ">="
             | "in" | "not in"
             | "starts_with" | "ends_with" | "contains"
             | "like"        ; glob, full match ( * ? )
             | "matches"     ; regex, full match
             | "under"       ; host == X or host ends_with "." + X
literal     := string | number [unit] | bool | list | ip | cidr | @list | method | "null"
list        := "[" literal ("," literal)* "]"
unit        := kb | mb | gb | ms | s | m | h      ; sizes are 1024-based
method      := [A-Z][A-Z_]*                       ; HTTP method names only A rule without when matches everything. So does a metric without
where.Strings are double-quoted, with \" and \\ escapes.Comparison is exact, except that host, tls.sni and scheme compare
without regard to case, and so do header names. Header values are
compared exactly. method is case-sensitive: get does not match
GET.Mistakes are compile errors: a type mismatch (host under 443), a
regex that does not compile, an unknown metric or @list, a
${secret:name} placeholder in a condition, or a comparison that can
never match, such as a host with a trailing dot or in upper case.
119.title: Expressions

120.text:
Admission fields are known when roxy decides whether to forward the
request. In-flight fields become known later, and a rule that reads one
is checked as the exchange streams
(evaluation). fieldtypeknownclient.ipipadmissionlistener.namestringadmissiontls.sni, tls.alpn, tls.versionstringadmissionmethod, scheme, host, port, path, urlstring / intadmissionquery["k"], query.rawstringadmissionheader["name"], header.all["name"]string, listadmissionbody.sizeint: declared length, null if not declaredadmissionbody.textstring: the buffered bodyadmissionmetric.<id>intadmission (rate limits)state["key"], tag["name"]string, booladmissionbody.bytesint: request body bytes so farin-flightresponse.status, response.header["name"], response.header.all["name"]int, string, listin-flightresponse.body.sizeint: declared length, null if not declaredin-flightresponse.body.textstring: the buffered response bodyin-flightresponse.body.bytesint: response body bytes so farin-flightws.direction, ws.opcode, ws.size, ws.textstring, int, int, stringin-flight, per WebSocket message (WebSockets) client.ip is the client's address, or behind a load balancer the one
X-Forwarded-For names
(HTTP). host and
tls.sni are lower-case, without a trailing dot, with internationalised
names as xn-- labels and IPv6 addresses without brackets. path is
normalised (URL normalisation). Path rules are fragile. An upstream may interpret a path differently
from roxy, for example by decoding %2F to / or merging //. Then
/a/..%2Fsecret does not start with /secret for roxy, but reaches
/secret upstream. Prefer allowing exact paths. If you allow a prefix,
also exclude the forms the upstream reinterprets (not path contains
"%2F", and likewise "%5C", "//", ";" and "%3B"). Treat a deny
on a path as defence in depth.
120.title: Fields

121.text:
A value that is absent is null: a header or query parameter that was not
sent, an unset state key, tls.sni when none was sent, body.size for a
chunked body. Tags and metrics are never null. expression, with x missingresultx == nulltruex != nullfalsex == "a", x in [...]falsex != "a", x not in [...]trueany other operator, such as x > 10 or x contains "a"the exchange is denied: _fail_closed, reason missing_value and and or stop as soon as the result is known, so test for null
first: body.size != null and body.size > 10mb, or
body.size == null or body.size > 1.
121.title: Missing values (null)

122.text:
then is one action, or a list ending with at most one of allow, deny
or quarantine. then: allow
then: { deny: { status: 451, message: "no" } }
then:
  - set_header: { authorization: "Bearer ${secret:openai}" }
  - remove_header: [x-debug]
  - tag: billing
  - allow: { upgrade: websocket } These decide the exchange: actionwhereeffectallowadmission rulesForward the request. upgrade: websocket allows a WebSocket upgrade. private_ok: true allows private addresses (address floor).denyall rulesRefuse, with status (default 403), message and close (deny responses). In flight, it stops the exchange. On a WebSocket, it closes both sides.quarantineall rulesDeny, and quarantine roxy so it refuses every later request. Needs --state-dir. These add effects: actionwhereeffectset_header: { name: value }request: admission rules; response: in-flight rulesSet or replace a header. Request values may use ${secret:name} (secrets).remove_header: [names]as set_headerRemove headers.rewrite_path: { match, to }admission rulesRewrite the path with a regex; $1 and ${name} refer to groups.set_query: { k: v }, remove_query: [k]admission rulesChange the query.redirect: { host, port, scheme?, rewrite_host? }admission rulesSend the request to another upstream. Host is unchanged unless rewrite_host: true. The new address still passes the address floor.tag: nameallSet tag["name"], for later rules, addons and the log.log: { level, message }allWrite a log event to the flow log.set_state: { key, value, ttl? }allWrite to the state store.capture: request | response | bothadmission rulesRecord the exchange in the capture log.digest: request | response | bothadmission rulesRecord a SHA-256 of the bodies in the flow log.sign: { aws_sigv4: { ... } }admission rulesSign the request for AWS (signing AWS requests). Anything more complex needs an addon.
122.title: Actions

123.text:
body.text and response.body.text are the only fields that make roxy
buffer. If any rule reads body.text, roxy buffers every request body, up
to limits.max_inspect_body_bytes (1 MiB), before deciding, then streams
it on. response.body.text does the same for responses. A body over the cap cannot be inspected, and a rule that reads it denies
the exchange (body_too_large_to_inspect). To let large bodies through,
raise the cap, or check the size before the text: when: body.size != null and body.size < 1mb and body.text contains "secret" The text is the body decoded from its content-encoding
(content codings). A body that cannot
be decoded also denies the exchange.
123.title: Body rules

124.text:
secrets: maps names to where their values come from. ${secret:name}
in a rule's set_header value, in sign credentials, or in an addon
endpoint's headers injects the value, so the client only ever holds a
placeholder. A reference anywhere else is a compile error. secrets:
  openai: { env: OPENAI_API_KEY }
  gh:     { file: /run/secrets/github_token }   # one trailing newline is stripped
  lease:  { lease: true }                       # supplied by the control plane

rules:
  - id: openai
    when: host == "api.openai.com" and path starts_with "/v1/" and method == POST
    then:
      - set_header: { authorization: "Bearer ${secret:openai}" }   # replaces whatever the client sent
      - allow Each secret has exactly one of env, file or lease: true.env and file are read at startup and on reload. A missing or empty
value stops roxy starting, or fails a reload. roxy check and
roxy rule test do not read them.Injected values are removed from the flow log and from captured headers.A redirect sends the request, injected values included, to the new
target. Make sure a rule that injects a secret cannot match a request
that another rule redirects elsewhere.
124.title: Secrets

125.text:
The sign action signs the forwarded request with AWS Signature Version
4, so a client holding placeholder credentials reaches AWS with a real
signature. secrets:
  aws_akid:  { env: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID }
  aws_sk:    { env: AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY }
  aws_token: { env: AWS_SESSION_TOKEN }

rules:
  - id: bedrock
    when: host under "bedrock-runtime.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com" and scheme == "https"
    then:
      - sign:
          aws_sigv4:
            service: bedrock
            region: eu-west-2
            access_key_id: "${secret:aws_akid}"
            secret_access_key: "${secret:aws_sk}"
            session_token: "${secret:aws_token}"   # optional
      - allow roxy signs the request as it is forwarded, after every other change the
rules make, wherever sign appears in then. It removes any signature
headers the client sent first.service is the AWS signing name, such as bedrock, s3 or
execute-api. S3 services get S3's variant of the signature.A request with a presigned URL (X-Amz-Signature in the query) is
forwarded under the client's signature, not roxy's. The rule's host
and path conditions still limit where it can go.The body is buffered, up to limits.max_sign_body_bytes (100 MiB), to
hash it. A larger body is refused with 413. For S3,
unsigned_payload: true skips the hash and streams the body.If two matching rules both sign, the request is denied
(sign_conflict).
125.title: Signing AWS requests

126.text:
name: { lease: true } declares a secret that the control plane supplies
with the lease (node protocol). It
is held in memory only, never on disk. roxy run --config refuses a
config that declares one. When the control plane changes a secret, the
next request uses the new value, while an exchange in progress keeps the
value it started with.
126.title: Lease secrets

127.text:
How roxy speaks TLS to clients on a proxy listener. Setting up the CA is
in managing the CA.
127.title: TLS

128.text:
roxy creates a certificate for each host the first time a client
connects to it, signed by its CA. Certificates are ECDSA P-256 and valid
for seven days, or until the CA expires if that is sooner. roxy keeps up
to tls.leaf_cache_size of them.
128.title: Leaf certificates

129.text:
roxy picks the certificate by SNI, or by the CONNECT host if the client
sends no SNI. An invalid SNI fails the handshake.Host names are compared in lower case without a trailing dot, so
CONNECT Example.COM.:443 with SNI example.com is one host.roxy offers HTTP/2 (with http.enable_h2) and HTTP/1.1.TLS 1.2 and 1.3 are supported. Sessions are not resumed.The handshake must finish within limits.header_timeout.
129.title: Client-facing TLS

130.text:
After a CONNECT, roxy reads the first TLS message to confirm that the
tunnel carries TLS and to find the SNI. A ClientHello that is malformed,
over 16 KiB, or split across several TLS records is treated as not TLS,
and the connection is closed.
130.title: ClientHello sniffing

131.text:
A kind: service addon is an external service that each exchange streams
through, at its place in the stack. roxy streams
the request to the service, and the service streams back the request to
forward, if it forwards one. roxy then streams the response from upstream
to the service, and the service streams back the response the client
gets. The service can pass bytes through, change them, hold them, or send
its own, in either direction, at any time. addons:
  - name: sentinel
    kind: service
    endpoint: sidecar                   # one of this addon's endpoints
    mode: enforce                       # enforce | observe
    endpoints:
      sidecar: { url: "http://127.0.0.1:9000/layer", private_ok: true }
    limits:
      first_byte_timeout: 2s
      max_connections: 4                # per endpoint
      max_streams: 100                  # exchanges at once per connection The other keys are as for any addon
(addon configuration). The quickstart's sidecar includes
roxy_layer.py,
a Python asyncio implementation of the service side of this protocol. It
handles the framing, flow control and errors, and hands a handler one
exchange at a time.
131.title: Service layer protocol

132.text:
roxy keeps long-lived WebSocket connections to the service, each carrying
many exchanges at once. Each exchange is a stream on a connection. The WebSocket subprotocol is roxy.layer.v7. A service that does not
accept it fails the handshake.roxy connects to the endpoint's URL (http becomes ws, https
becomes wss), checked by the address floor, with the endpoint's
headers.A new exchange uses an idle connection if there is one, otherwise opens
a new one up to max_connections, otherwise shares the least busy
connection. Each connection is read and written in order, so a service
that handles each connection on one task gets one core per connection.If a connection fails, the exchanges on it fail. Later exchanges use
another connection.After a reload, new exchanges use new connections, and old connections
close once their exchanges finish.
132.title: Transport

133.text:
Text frames are JSON messages, each with a stream field. Binary frames
are body bytes: a 4-byte big-endian stream id, one byte for the direction
(0 request body, 1 response body), then the bytes. roxy numbers the
streams on a connection from 1 upwards and never reuses a number. A stream starts with an open message from roxy: {"type":"open","stream":7,"flow":"01J…","conn":"01J…","layer":"sentinel",
 "mode":"enforce","subscribe":{"request":"full","response":"head"},
 "client_ip":"10.0.0.5","listener":"proxy",
 "sni":"api.example.com","tags":["a","b"],
 "capabilities":["state","record"],"config":{"reject_at":0.8}} client_ip is client.ip as rules see it. sni is left out when there
is none. capabilities and config are the addon's. flow and layer
together identify the exchange and addon, so a service can key its state
on them. The rest of the exchange, with stream left out: roxy → service   {"type":"request","method":…,"url":…,"headers":[[n,v],…]}  bytes…  {"type":"request_end"}
service → roxy   {"type":"request",…}  bytes…  {"type":"request_end"}       the request to forward, at most once
                 {"type":"request_end"} alone                             forward nothing
roxy → service   {"type":"response","status":…,"headers":[…]}  bytes…  {"type":"response_end"}
                                                                          the response to what the service forwarded
                 {"type":"response_end"} alone                            no response: nothing was forwarded, or the forward failed
service → roxy   {"type":"response",…}  bytes…  {"type":"response_end"}   the client's response, exactly once
either way       {"type":"trailers","dir":"request"|"response","headers":[…]}  trailers, after the body
                 {"type":"stop","dir":"request"|"response"}               "I will read no more of this body"
                 {"type":"credit","dir":"request"|"response","bytes":n}  flow control (below)
                 {"type":"reset","message":"…"}                           abandon the stream
service → roxy   host-service calls (below)
roxy → service   {"type":"result","id":n,"value":…} or {"type":"result","id":n,"error":"…"} So each stream carries four HTTP messages: the request into the service,
the request out of it, the response into it and the response out of it.
Each message is a head, then body bytes, then optional trailers, then an
end, in that order. ruledetailheadsurl is absolute. headers are the end-to-end headers, with no hop-by-hop or framing fields, and at most limits.max_headers of them. If the service sends content-length, its body must match itheader valuesstrings in which each character is one byte (ISO-8859-1)trailersrequest trailers from the service follow the rules for a client's (trailers)orderthe four messages are independent. The service can send its response before, during or without forwarding the requesterrorsan end message may carry "error", meaning the body stopped early and is incomplete. When the service does this to its own message it is not a fault: the flow log records layer_aborted, unless a fault or the client leaving came firststopstop tells the other side to send no more of that body. When the service stops reading the response, the upstream request is cancelledend of streamthe stream ends when all four messages have ended or been stopped and all host-service calls have been answered. Either side can abandon it with reset, and a reset from the service fails an enforcing exchangeflow controleach body starts with 256 KiB of credit in each direction. The receiver grants more with credit as it reads. Sending more than the credit allows is a protocol error. Messages other than body bytes are not countedhead-onlywhen subscribe is head for a direction, roxy sends only the head and the service answers with only a head (or with an end alone, to send nothing). The body bypasses the service. Bytes, trailers or an end after the head fail the exchange (unsubscribed:<direction>)
133.title: Frames

134.text:
A service reaches the same host services as a
WASM addon, by message, with the same capabilities. Each call has an id
chosen by the service (an unsigned 64-bit integer), and roxy answers with
a result carrying the same id: value is the answer (null for
calls that return nothing), and error says the call was refused. service → roxycapabilityroxy → service{"type":"log","id":n,"level":"info","message":"…"} (trace, debug, info, warn, error)log{"type":"result","id":n,"value":null}{"type":"record","id":n,"kind":"…","data":<json>}record{"type":"result","id":n,"value":null}{"type":"add_tag","id":n,"tag":"…"}none; enforce only{"type":"result","id":n,"value":null}{"type":"state_get","id":n,"key":"…"}state{"type":"result","id":n,"value":"…"} (null if not set){"type":"state_put","id":n,"key":"…","value":"…","ttl_ms":n?}state; enforce only{"type":"result","id":n,"value":null}{"type":"metric_get","id":n,"metric":"…"}metrics{"type":"result","id":n,"value":n} (null if no count yet){"type":"quarantine","id":n}quarantine; enforce only{"type":"result","id":n,"value":null} Calls can be sent at any time while the stream is open. They run one at a
time, in order, alongside the bodies, not in sequence with them. If an
effect must happen before something else, such as a tag before the
request is forwarded, wait for its result before sending that
(ordering across layers).
At most 64 calls can be waiting at once. A call without its capability, a message over 64 KiB, or a tag or state
write from an observer fails the addon and resets the stream. The flow
log records the call's id as call on the events it causes. A service
makes endpoint calls itself, so there is no message for them.
134.title: Host services

135.text: roxy offers only roxy.layer.v7. WASM addons use roxy:addon@0.3.0.
135.title: Versions

136.text:
The forwarded request is checked and judged by the rules, as a WASM
addon's is. The response that comes back may be the upstream's, a
refusal from the rules, or an error for a failure upstream. The service
can pass any of these on or change them.Deadlines. first_byte_timeout runs from roxy's request head until
the service answers or forwards. It pauses while the forwarded request
is upstream, and starts again in full when the response arrives. There
is no overall deadline on a stream, but body idle timeouts apply.An early response goes to the client at once. The upstream's
response still arrives for the service to read, and the service's
answer stands whatever happens upstream.Failure is closed. In enforce mode, a failed connection, a protocol
error (bad JSON, a message out of order, a bad head, too many bytes), a
missed deadline or a reset fails the exchange with 503 if the
response has not started, and ends the response early if it has. The
layer_error kind is service:connect, service:protocol,
service:timeout or service:closed. A response_end with no
response before it is no_response.A body that fails on its way to the service is not its fault. Its
end carries the error, and the stream carries on.A protocol error affects one stream, unless the framing itself is
broken (a text frame that is not a JSON object with a valid stream, a
short binary frame, an unknown stream). Then the whole connection fails.Observe mode streams go one way. roxy sends copies of the request
and response. The service sends only credit, stop, host-service
calls, reset, and {"type":"close"} when it is done, which must come
within first_byte_timeout of roxy's last message. Waiting for credit
is falling behind, so grant generous credit when an observe stream
opens.WebSockets run through the stream. The upstream's 101 arrives as
the response head, and the service answers with a 101 of its own.
After that, the request body carries the client's bytes and the
response body the upstream's, until each side closes. roxy sends no
request_end before the 101, so the service must forward the upgrade
as it arrives rather than waiting for the request to end.
136.title: Semantics

137.text:
How roxy reaches the origin: it resolves names itself, checks every
address against the address floor,
and verifies the origin's TLS certificate. upstream:
  dns:
    resolver: system           # system | [ "1.1.1.1:53", ... ]
    cache_ttl_cap: 60s         # the longest roxy caches an answer
    static_hosts: {}           # name: ip, used before DNS; still checked by the address floor
  deny_private_ranges: true
  deny_cidrs: []               # never connect to these
  allow_cidrs: []              # exceptions to the private ranges only
  deny_lists: [blocked]        # names from address_lists
  connect_timeout: 10s         # for the TCP connection, then again for the TLS handshake
  max_h2_connections_per_origin: 4

tls:
  upstream:
    verify: strict             # strict | strict+extra_roots
    extra_roots: []            # PEM files
    min_version: "1.2"         # "1.2" | "1.3" deny_cidrs and allow_cidrs entries must be networks: roxy check
refuses 10.1.2.3/8 and suggests 10.0.0.0/8.
137.title: Upstream

138.text:
roxy resolves upstream names itself, so the workload's DNS plays no part.
If a name has several addresses, roxy tries them in turn, alternating
IPv4 and IPv6, within one connect_timeout. The resolver is set up at
startup, so changing upstream.dns needs a
restart.
138.title: DNS

139.text:
roxy verifies every upstream certificate against the Mozilla root
certificates, plus extra_roots with verify: strict+extra_roots.
Verification cannot be turned off. The TLS handshake has its own
connect_timeout.
139.title: Upstream TLS

140.text:
roxy keeps connections to each origin open for reuse, and closes them
after 90 seconds idle. Over HTTP/1.1 it opens one connection per request
in progress. Over HTTP/2 it uses up to max_h2_connections_per_origin
connections and spreads requests across them. If an HTTP/2 origin closes a connection before handling some requests,
roxy retries those without a body on another connection. A request with
a body gets 502, since its body has already been sent.
140.title: Connections

141.text:
failureresponseflow logthe address floor refuses the address403, _address_policyupstream_deniedDNS, connection or TLS failure502upstream_error, reason dns_failed, connect_failed or tls_faileda target roxy cannot connect to502upstream_error, reason invalid_targeta timeout connecting, during the TLS handshake or waiting for the response504upstream_error, reason timeouta response roxy cannot parse502upstream_error, reason protocol_error The client gets the usual refusal body
(deny responses). The reason is in the
flow log only.
141.title: Errors

142.text:
On a proxy listener roxy terminates every TLS connection with a
certificate signed by its own CA, so clients must trust that CA. roxy
generates the CA, or uses one you provide. The certificates it signs are
described in TLS. ca_server:
  bind: 0.0.0.0:3130           # serves /roxy-ca.pem and the health checks; absent = off

tls:
  ca_dir: /var/lib/roxy/ca     # roxy-ca.pem + roxy-ca.key, generated if absent
  # ca_cert: /etc/roxy/ca/tls.crt  # a CA you provide instead; set both or neither
  # ca_key: /etc/roxy/ca/tls.key
  require_sni_match: true
  leaf_cache_size: 10000       # at least 1
142.title: Managing the CA

143.text:
On first roxy run, or roxy ca init, roxy generates an ECDSA P-256 CA
valid for 10 years. It writes roxy-ca.pem and roxy-ca.key (mode 0600)
to tls.ca_dir, and reuses them on later starts. A corrupt pair stops
roxy rather than being replaced, since a new CA breaks every client's
trust. roxy ca init --force replaces it on purpose.
143.title: Generated CA

144.text:
Set tls.ca_cert and tls.ca_key to use a CA you already have, such as
a sub-CA of your organisation's root or a Kubernetes tls secret. ca_cert is PEM. The first certificate is the CA. Any further
certificates are its intermediates, in order, without the root. roxy
sends them to clients so that clients trusting only the root can build
the chain.ca_key is the CA's private key as unencrypted PKCS#8 PEM
(BEGIN PRIVATE KEY). roxy is tested with ECDSA P-256 keys. To convert
another key format:
openssl pkcs8 -topk8 -nocrypt -in ca.key -out ca-pkcs8.key. roxy never generates or replaces a provided CA.
144.title: Provided CA

145.text:
At startup, and in roxy check, roxy checks that the CA is a valid CA
certificate within its validity period and matches its key. Any failure
stops roxy. It warns when the key file is readable by other users, and
when the CA expires within seven days. Once the CA has expired, every TLS
handshake fails.
145.title: Startup checks

146.text:
The CA certificate, never the key, can be fetched three ways. For a
provided CA this is the CA alone, without intermediates. roxy ca export --config roxy.yaml > roxy-ca.pem                   # at image build time (--der for DER)
curl -s http://<ca_server.bind>/roxy-ca.pem > roxy-ca.pem         # from the CA server
curl -s -x http://<proxy> http://roxy.internal/roxy-ca.pem        # through the proxy itself The ca_server listener is separate from the proxy port so it can be
firewalled separately.
146.title: CA distribution

147.text:
roxy only allows a WebSocket upgrade when the allowing rule says
allow: { upgrade: websocket }. Under a plain allow, roxy removes the
upgrade headers and forwards the request as ordinary HTTP, so the
client's WebSocket library reports a failed handshake. Upgrades to other
protocols are always removed.
147.title: WebSockets

148.text:
roxy forwards the upgrade over HTTP/1.1 and sends the client the 101
only once the upstream has accepted, so a failed upgrade is always an
error response. failureresultthe client's upgrade request is not a valid WebSocket handshake400, terminal_rule: _websocket, reason ws_bad_handshakethe upstream does not answer within limits.response_header_timeout504the upstream answers something other than 101passed to the client as it isthe upstream's 101 is invalid502 Through a proxy listener, use wss://. A ws:// URL means plain HTTP
inside a CONNECT tunnel, which roxy refuses unless
http.allow_plain_in_connect is on. WebSockets over HTTP/2 are not
supported, so clients use HTTP/1.1 for them. If no rule reads a ws.* field, roxy passes the bytes through as they
are. Either way: WebSocket bytes count towards byte metrics, so a byte limit can close a
WebSocket.Capture records both directions.Addons sit between the client and the relay, so rules and capture see
what the addons pass on.A WebSocket with no traffic for limits.idle_timeout (1 h) is closed.The flow log records ws_open and ws_close, with byte counts.
148.title: Relay

149.text:
A compressed WebSocket message cannot be read on its own, so when
anything needs to read messages, roxy removes the client's offer of
compression. That is when a rule reads ws.*, or when an addon runs on
the upgrade and decodes bodies (the default;
addons). Otherwise
extensions pass through.
149.title: Extensions

150.text:
Rules that read ws.* are checked on every message after the upgrade: rules:
  - id: chat
    when: host == "chat.example.com"
    then: { allow: { upgrade: websocket } }
  - id: no-keys-out
    when: ws.direction == "c2s" and ws.opcode == 1 and ws.text matches ".*sk-[A-Za-z0-9]{20,}.*"
    then: deny fieldvaluews.directionc2s (client to upstream) or s2cws.opcode1 text, 2 binary, 8 close, 9 ping, 10 pongws.sizepayload length in bytesws.texta text message's text; null for other messages ws.text is null for pings and other control messages, so start text
rules with ws.opcode == 1 and ...
(missing values).
Otherwise the first ping closes the WebSocket. A matching deny closes both sides with code 1008. Rules cannot drop or
change a single message; that needs an addon.
150.title: Message rules

151.text:
With message rules, roxy checks each message strictly against the
WebSocket spec, reassembles fragmented messages up to
limits.max_ws_message_bytes (16 MiB), and checks that text is valid
UTF-8. It forwards each message once it is complete, as a single frame.
A protocol error closes both sides with 1002, 1007 for invalid UTF-8,
or 1009 for a message over the limit.
151.title: Parsing

152.text:
A denied message is logged as a ws_message event. With
log.flow.ws_message_every: N, every Nth message is logged as well.
Message contents are never logged.
152.title: Logging

153.text:
An untrusted workload runs where its only route out is roxy. It sends its
traffic to roxy's proxy port and trusts roxy's CA. The network does the
containing: the proxy settings only tell a well-behaved client where roxy
is (threat model).
153.title: Sandbox containment

154.text:
Take away the workload's route out. Put it in a network namespace,
VM or container network where roxy is the only host it can reach.
Block everything else, including DNS. roxy resolves names itself, so
the workload needs no DNS.Give roxy a route out, and give the workload a route to roxy's
proxy port. Let the workload reach the CA port too if it should fetch
the CA itself.listeners:
  - name: proxy
    mode: http_proxy
    bind: 0.0.0.0:3128
ca_server:
  bind: 0.0.0.0:3130             # serves /roxy-ca.pemPoint the workload at roxy and make it trust roxy's CA
(CA distribution):export HTTP_PROXY=http://<proxy> HTTPS_PROXY=http://<proxy>
export http_proxy=$HTTP_PROXY https_proxy=$HTTPS_PROXY   # curl reads only the lower-case http_proxy
export SSL_CERT_FILE=/path/roxy-ca.pem         # OpenSSL-based tools, Python ssl, Go
export REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE=/path/roxy-ca.pem    # Python requests
export NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS=/path/roxy-ca.pem   # Node
export CURL_CA_BUNDLE=/path/roxy-ca.pem        # curlAdding the certificate to the system trust store also works. Do not put
external hosts in NO_PROXY.Optionally, shut roxy for good when the workload misbehaves. A
quarantine refuses every request until
an operator lifts it. It can be tripped by a rule, or by a run of
malformed requests:listeners:
  - name: proxy
    bind: 0.0.0.0:3128
    quarantine_on:
      parse_errors: { count: 20, window: 1m }
rules:
  - id: exfil
    when: host == "api.anthropic.com" and body.text contains "BEGIN PRIVATE KEY"
    then: quarantineRun roxy with --state-dir so the quarantine survives a restart.
154.title: Steps

155.text:
The workload is only on an internal: true network, which has no route
out. roxy is on that network and on one with a route out: services:
  roxy:
    image: ghcr.io/roxy-proxy/roxy:latest
    read_only: true
    cap_drop: [ALL]
    security_opt: ["no-new-privileges:true"]
    volumes: [./roxy.yaml:/etc/roxy/roxy.yaml:ro, roxy-ca:/var/lib/roxy/ca]
    networks: [sandbox, egress]
  agent:
    image: your-workload
    networks: [sandbox]              # no route out except through roxy
    environment:
      HTTPS_PROXY: http://roxy:3128
      https_proxy: http://roxy:3128
      NO_PROXY: roxy                 # roxy's CA endpoint, reached directly
      no_proxy: roxy
networks:
  sandbox:
    internal: true                   # no route out: the containment
  egress: {}
volumes:
  roxy-ca: {} The workload fetches the CA from http://roxy:3130/roxy-ca.pem. A client
that ignores the proxy settings gets nowhere, because there is no route
out. Other services on the Compose network have private addresses, which roxy
refuses by default. A rule that lets the workload reach one needs
then: { allow: { private_ok: true } }
(address floor).
155.title: With Docker Compose

156.text:
An http listener lets roxy stand in for an origin. Clients send ordinary
requests to a name that resolves to roxy, and rules decide where each one
goes and what to add. The example here is an LLM gateway: clients hold
placeholder keys, and roxy adds the real ones on the way out.
156.title: HTTP gateway

157.text:
*.gw.example.com points at a load balancer, which terminates TLS and
forwards plain HTTP to roxy. One rule per subdomain redirects the request
to its provider over HTTPS and sets the real key. Anything no rule
matches is denied. version: 1

listeners:
  - name: gateway
    mode: http
    bind: 0.0.0.0:8080
    forwarded_for: { trusted_hops: 1 }   # one load balancer in front

secrets:
  anthropic: { env: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }
  openai:    { env: OPENAI_API_KEY }
  aws_akid:  { env: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID }
  aws_sk:    { env: AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY }

rules:
  - id: anthropic
    when: listener.name == "gateway" and host == "anthropic.gw.example.com" and path starts_with "/v1/"
    then:
      - redirect: { host: api.anthropic.com, port: 443, scheme: https, rewrite_host: true }
      - set_header: { x-api-key: "${secret:anthropic}" }
      - allow

  - id: openai
    when: listener.name == "gateway" and host == "openai.gw.example.com" and path starts_with "/v1/"
    then:
      - redirect: { host: api.openai.com, port: 443, scheme: https, rewrite_host: true }
      - set_header: { authorization: "Bearer ${secret:openai}" }
      - allow

  - id: bedrock
    when: listener.name == "gateway" and host == "bedrock.gw.example.com" and path starts_with "/model/"
    then:
      - redirect: { host: bedrock-runtime.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com, port: 443, scheme: https, rewrite_host: true }
      - sign:
          aws_sigv4:
            service: bedrock
            region: eu-west-2
            access_key_id: "${secret:aws_akid}"
            secret_access_key: "${secret:aws_sk}"
      - allow rewrite_host: true sends the provider's name in Host, which the
provider expects (redirect).
Bedrock needs a signature rather than a key. sign signs the request as
forwarded, after the redirect
(signing AWS requests).
157.title: The pattern

158.text:
The listener does no authentication: rules see only listener.name and
client.ip. Authenticate clients at the load balancer, or with an addon
that checks a credential and tags the exchange with the user, as the
quickstart's auth check does
(what just happened). A per-user quota
is another addon.
158.title: Authenticating clients

159.text:
This is not containment. The listener serves whoever reaches it,
and clients may have other routes out
(threat model).Say how many proxies are in front. Set
forwarded_for.trusted_hops to the number of proxies between clients
and roxy, so client.ip is the real client rather than the load
balancer (HTTP). Only
the load balancer may be able to reach the listener: a client that
connects directly can choose its own client.ip.Leave the per-client connection cap alone. It counts the load
balancer, not the client, so lowering it caps the whole gateway
(limits).TLS stays at the load balancer. roxy does not terminate TLS on an
http listener, so keep the hop from the load balancer to roxy on a
network you trust.In-cluster upstreams have private addresses, which roxy refuses by
default. A rule that forwards to one needs
then: { allow: { private_ok: true } }
(address floor).Do not use quarantine. A quarantine
shuts the whole process, so one client's bad requests would lock out
every other client.
159.title: What to know

160.text:
roxy's own logs go to stderr (--log-format json|pretty, --log-level
or RUST_LOG). The flow log goes to stdout or a file
(flow log). SIGHUP reloads the config and reopens
log files. SIGTERM or Ctrl-C stops accepting connections, lets
exchanges in flight finish for up to 10 seconds, and flushes the logs
before exiting.
160.title: Operations

161.text:
The ca_server listener answers two checks: path200 whenotherwise/healthzthe process is upno answer/readyza policy is loaded, it has not expired, and roxy is not quarantined503 with the reason: no_policy, policy_expired or quarantined /healthz also sends x-roxy-policy: valid, expired or quarantined.
Use /healthz for liveness and /readyz for readiness. An empty policy
counts as ready: it denies everything, on purpose. no_policy is only
seen in node mode, before the first lease arrives. roxy health checks http://127.0.0.1:3130/healthz for images without
curl. --ready checks /readyz instead and --url sets the address. It
exits 0 on a 200 and 1 otherwise. ca_server has its own connection cap. Keep its port reachable only from
the health checks and the workloads that fetch the CA, since a client that
fills the cap blocks the checks.
161.title: Health

162.text:
roxy check --config <file> validates a config without starting roxy: it
parses it, compiles the rules and addons, and loads the address lists and
a provided CA. It does not read secrets from the environment. roxy watches the config file, the address-list files and the addon
.wasm files, and reloads when one changes or on SIGHUP. A reload that
succeeds is applied at once: exchanges in flight finish under the old
policy, and the next request uses the new one. A reload that fails
changes nothing, and logs a config_reload_failed event with the
diagnostics. Rate-limit counters survive a reload when their metric is unchanged
(metrics).
162.title: Reload

163.text:
Some settings take effect only when roxy starts: listeners, ca_server, tls.ca_dir, tls.ca_cert, tls.ca_key, tls.leaf_cache_size, tls.upstream, upstream.dns, limits.max_connections, limits.max_connections_per_client, limits.max_state_entries, limits.max_capture_body_bytes, log.flow, log.capture and capture_dir. A reload keeps their running values, applies everything else, and warns about each one that changed. Connection-level settings, such as the HTTP parsing limits and timeouts,
are fixed when a connection is accepted. A reload changes them for new
connections only.
163.title: Restart-only settings

164.text:
A top-level valid_until: <RFC 3339 time> makes the policy expire. From
that moment every request is denied with terminal_rule: _expired, and
open WebSockets are closed. /healthz stays up and /readyz answers
503 policy_expired. To recover, load a config with a later valid_until, or none. There is
no fallback policy. In node mode the control plane
sets valid_until from its lease.
164.title: Lease

165.text:
A quarantine makes roxy refuse every request, whatever the policy says,
until someone lifts it from outside the process. It is for a workload
that has shown itself hostile. It survives reloads and restarts. Three things can trip it: a rule's quarantine action
(actions);an addon calling flow.quarantine
(host services);a listener's quarantine_on.parse_errors threshold: that many
malformed requests within the window
(listener modes). Timeouts and
clients that disconnect do not count. Use it on a sandbox's listener,
never a gateway's. While quarantined, every request is refused with 403 and
terminal_rule: _quarantined. Open connections are closed after one
second. The trip is logged as a quarantined event with an incident id
(flow log). /readyz answers
503 quarantined, and the CA is still served. A config that can quarantine needs roxy run --state-dir DIR. The trip
writes DIR/quarantine, and roxy starts quarantined while that file
exists. To lift it, stop roxy, remove DIR/quarantine and start it again.
In node mode the control plane lifts it
instead.
165.title: Quarantine

166.text:
In node mode roxy has no config file. It enrols with a control plane,
leases its policy and secrets from it, and sends its flow log back. The
control plane is any server that implements the
node protocol. roxy run --control-plane https://cp.example:8443 \
         --enrol-token-file /run/secrets/roxy-enrol-token \
         --state-dir /var/lib/roxy/node \
         --control-plane-ca /etc/roxy/cp-ca.pem
166.title: Node mode

167.text:
flagmeaning--control-plane URLThe control plane's https:// URL. Cannot be combined with --config.--enrol-token-file PATHThe enrolment token. Only read when the state dir holds no node token yet.--state-dir DIRWhere the node keeps its token, its CA and its quarantine marker.--control-plane-ca PATHCA certificates to verify the control plane with. Default: the system roots.--bootstrap-bind ADDRWhere the proxy listens before the first lease. Default 0.0.0.0:3128.--bootstrap-ca-server ADDRWhere ca_server listens before the first lease. Default 0.0.0.0:3130.--interception-ca-cert PATH, --interception-ca-key PATHA CA to use instead of generating one (the interception CA).--replace-interception-caReplace a stored CA that differs from the one given. The control plane decides how long an enrolment token lasts and whether it
can be reused. roxy does not delete the token file.
167.title: Flags

168.text:
The state dir holds the node token, a flow sequence counter, the CA in
ca/, and a quarantine file while the node is quarantined. The rendered
config and secrets stay in memory only. A copy of the state dir is a copy
of the node's identity, which the control plane can revoke.
168.title: The state dir

169.text:
The CA always lives in <state-dir>/ca. On first start roxy generates
one, or imports the pair given with --interception-ca-cert and
--interception-ca-key. After that the stored CA is used. If the flags
name a different pair, roxy refuses to start, since workloads already
trust the stored CA. Pass --replace-interception-ca to replace it. Workloads fetch the CA from ca_server as usual
(CA distribution).
169.title: The interception CA

170.text:
The listeners open at once with an empty policy, so every request is
denied and /readyz answers 503 no_policy.Without a stored node token, the node enrols with the enrolment token.
If the control plane refuses it, the node retries for two minutes and
then exits, so an orchestrator sees a crash loop. An unreachable
control plane is retried for as long as it takes.The node fetches its lease and applies it. Settings that only apply at
startup (restart-only settings)
are taken from the first lease. A later lease that changes one is
logged and needs a restart.
170.title: Startup

171.text:
Every lease is the whole policy, applied in full or not at all. A lease
that roxy check would reject, or that lacks a secret the config needs, is
logged and the running policy stays. The lease sets the policy's expiry (lease),
measured on the node's own clock. The node polls again before it runs
out. If the control plane is unreachable, the lease expires and roxy
denies everything until the next successful poll, with no restart needed. A revoked node (410) denies everything at once and stops polling. A
node never enrols again on its own. To re-enrol it, empty the state dir
and start it with a new enrolment token. A quarantined node keeps applying
leases. It reports the quarantine on every poll, and lifts it when the
control plane releases that incident in a lease. The node renews its token before it expires. If the token does expire,
the node exits, since only re-enrolment can recover it.
171.title: The lease

172.text:
Every flow-log event goes to the local flow log as usual, and to the
control plane in batches, as the lease's flow settings say
(flow upload). Events wait in
memory until the control plane acknowledges them. When too many are
waiting, the lease decides whether roxy holds traffic (hold) or drops the
oldest events (spool). On shutdown roxy ships what is waiting, for up to
ten seconds. SIGHUP reopens the local log files. Health checks work as in
operations: ready means an unexpired lease is
in force.
172.title: Flow shipping

176.text:
roxy check validates a config. roxy rule test shows what the policy
does with a request you describe, without sending any traffic. roxy check --config roxy.yaml        # exits 1 with diagnostics

roxy rule test --config roxy.yaml --metric github_writes=30 POST https://api.github.com/repos/a/b/issues roxy rule test prints the matching rules, their effects and the
decision. It exits 0 on allow and 3 on deny. The request arrives on the
config's first listener. The rules see the request as roxy run would: the URL is normalised
(https://H.example./a/%2e/b/../c has host == "h.example" and
path == "/a/c"), and a request roxy would refuse as malformed exits 1
